extracted.intended_audience: general readers and practitioners interested in horse husbandry (horse owners, farmers, farriers, veterinarians)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for judging horse-foot care and shoeing practice—when shoes are necessary, what forms are harmful or beneficial, and environmental/management practices that affect hoof health. Covers empirical examples, historical authorities, and economic and welfare arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural barefoot adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature intended the horse to walk barefoot; the natural sole is almost impenetrable and fitted to stand all wear and tear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument supported by observations (Exmoor, Dartmoor, Orkneys, Welsh hills, continental Europe), classical authorities (Xenophon, Vegetius), and examples of unshod animals (mustangs). Emphasises that differences in soil quality are of comparatively little importance if the hoof is allowed to function naturally. Anti-pattern: assuming hard modern roads require iron protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of nails and nail-attached shoes
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of attaching shoes by nails is injurious to the hoof and is probably the cause of many affections of the foot and leg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides graphic examples of laceration, compression, and damage caused by nails (e.g., multiple nails driven into quarters, carving out crust for clips). Scoring/inspection note: presence of nail wounds, scars, or lacerated crusts indicate harmful practice. Anti-pattern: accepting lameness as due to anything other than shoe-caused injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize added weight on the hoof
rubrics_metrics.description: Each additional ounce on the horse's foot makes a most sensible difference in the amount of work performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares weights of shoes (ordinary shoe vs. Seeley's patent vs. reduced Charlier forms). Preference for lighter or reduced shoes when metal must be used. Economic/efficiency implication: lighter feet lead to increased endurance and comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow natural expansion and contraction of the foot
rubrics_metrics.description: Shoes should not interfere with the natural expansion and contraction process of the hoof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that a shoe which encircles or is fixed into parts of the foot beyond the wall prevents natural movement (malleable iron has no spring). Anti-pattern: shoes let into the crust that extend into the bars and prevent normal hoof dynamics; such shoes may twist or break under exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer minimal/tip protection over full metal shoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where some protection is required, the use of a small iron 'tip' or minimal fragment (rather than a full heavy shoe) may be sufficient and less harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Mayhew and practical users who retain only a small curled piece of iron at the toe, or use modified Charlier/three-quarter shoes. Examples: farmers and American users reporting success with minimal protection for animals with abused feet. Anti-pattern: defaulting to full iron sets for all horses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable and yard surface should be hard/irregular to strengthen hoof
rubrics_metrics.description: Stable-floors must not be smooth or damp; they should be lined with irregular stones of sizes similar to the hoof to strengthen the frog and encourage hoof hardening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws on Xenophon's prescriptions: loose stones in parts of the ground, surrounded to prevent scattering, produce the condition of traveling on stony roads and strengthen the feet. Anti-pattern: constant litter or soft bedding that makes feet tender and causes swollen legs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pare the sole
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural sole protects the sensitive sole from harm, provided that the sole is never pared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that exposure to hard objects actually hardens the sole; paring undermines this protective function. Inspection criterion: overly pared soles suggest misguided farriery and increased vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical cross-climate evidence supports unshod practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Long experience in diverse countries (America, Mexico, Peru, Brazil, India, etc.) shows unshod horses working over many miles and various roads without wearing out hooves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses military, agricultural, and transport examples (cavalry in the Indian Mutiny, horses in American and Continental contexts, Cortes' horses, mustangs) as empirical evidence. Reviewers should weigh such empirical case histories when assessing claims about necessity of shoeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shoeing is a principal cause of many hoof diseases and lameness
rubrics_metrics.description: A very large proportion of troubles in horses' feet can be traced to shoeing—leading to contracted feet, corns, sand-cracks, and other maladies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes practitioners (e.g., 'nine hundred and ninety-nine thousandths of all the trouble in horses' feet come from shoeing') and veterinary opinion (The Lancet). Anti-pattern: attributing these conditions to climate or road surfaces instead of shoeing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition away from shoeing should be cautious and gradual
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformers warn against imprudent haste; improvements may be achieved without immediate and complete abandonment of shoeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical example: removing shoes and giving a month's rest with occasional short drives; initial chipping followed by the hoof growing thicker and harder and returning to work. Scoring note: successful transitions often involve a period of rest/pasture for hoof hardening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified or reduced shoes can be a pragmatic improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced-size or specially designed shoes (e.g., Charlier modifications, Seeley's patent) that lessen contact and weight can confer benefits compared to traditional full shoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes Charlier's narrow iron, Melton's three-quarter reduction (five ounces), and Seeley's one-pound quarter shoe used by tramway companies; cites practical users (Smither & Son) reporting comfort and safety across pavements and roads. Anti-pattern: treating any metal shoe as equally acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unshod horses perform well on varied surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Unshod horses can successfully deal with all roads—soft, hard, stony, slippery, or icy—and may outperform shod horses in many conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides concrete examples: galloping on ice, trotting miles on hard flint roads, firm treading on slime of wood pavement, and cavalry/retreat examples where horses lost shoes yet performed. Evaluation should consider functional outcomes (slipping, endurance, soundness) on target surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and welfare benefits of abandoning shoeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandoning shoeing promises large economic savings (reduced farriery bills, medicines, straw) and improved welfare (longer-lived, more comfortable horses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims potential national-level savings and per-horse yearly savings; also notes decreased veterinary costs and removal of many diseases. Anti-pattern: focusing solely on short-term disruption to farriers without considering long-term savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fashion-driven or excessive farriery practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamental or fashion-driven practices (e.g., carving out the crust, adding high calks/cogs) can be extremely harmful and amount to cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples of farriers and veterinary surgeons applying extreme fittings (three-quarter-inch calks, screw cogs, carving for clips) and warns against regarding such manipulations with satisfaction. Inspection criterion: detect unnecessary alterations or decorative fittings that compromise hoof integrity.
